enquiry: We would like an optical measurement during yeast fermentation to help us follow growth and notice changes earlier. Our team has mentioned both a biomass signal and a metabolic signal, but these have not been defined as separate targets. The broth becomes more optically dense as the run develops. We need help turning this request into an initial feasibility study with useful reference measurements.

solution_options.fusion_note: Start from one model per method, UV-Vis for biomass and Raman for metabolites, then fuse the two spectral blocks at the low level with autoscaling so neither method dominates. Both probes must look at the same broth point and the two data streams must be normalised to a common time step before fusion. The fused model must beat the best single method on held-out runs, or the second instrument is not worth keeping.

assessment.chemometrics_note: Both targets need calibration or classification models built on reference data, and NIR and Raman calibrations are specific to the sample matrix, so the models must be re-validated if the broth composition changes.
assessment.realtime_tracking_note: Fiber probes give near-real-time in-line results without sampling; if both methods run together, their data must be aligned to a common time step before fusion.
assessment.future_direction: Once the key wavelengths for a single fixed target are known, a compact spectral fiber or LED sensor could replace full spectrometers for routine control.

proposal.what_would_change_it: If the metabolic signal turns out to be a fluorescent species, fluorescence would join the shortlist; if the broth stays optically thin enough, UV-Vis transmission could replace the ATR geometry and become the simplest first test.
proposal.next_step: Agree the reference methods and the go/no-go numbers with the customer, then run the single-method tests on representative broth samples.

assessment.brief_answer: Test the single methods first on representative broth: Raman for the metabolic signal and UV-Vis for the growth signal, each against an independent reference. Raman suits the aqueous broth; UV-Vis turbidity tracks cell density but is not a cell count. Which species the metabolic signal is, and whether the broth stays optically thin enough for transmission, are still open and decide the method. A combined Raman and UV-Vis option is a later hypothesis to test.
